title: Learning the Fermion sign structure in path-integral Monte Carlo
abstract: Starting from a \emph{probabilistic numerics} approach to the Fermion sign problem in path integral Monte Carlo, we recast the arithmetic calculation of a Fermionic observable as a statistical inference problem. We develop approaches that learn the behaviour of Fermion exchange cycles binned by the conjugacy class of the permutation group (which we term `permutation family'). This extends the work of DuBois, Brown and Alder\cite{dubois2017overcoming} to inhomogeneous and more complex systems. Monte Carlo samples are used to train models for both the probability of a permutation family and the energy of this set of exchange permutations. The overall Fermionic energy is then directly inferred from these models, without using a direct ratio estimator on the Monte Carlo samples.   By imposing physical understanding as inductive priors, we produce accurate and useful fits that remain robust even in regimes with severe sign problems. We generalise the linear (ideal-gas style) models of DuBois et al. with Bayesian priors that enforce the intuitive models of Feynman\cite{Feynman1953A} at their asymptotic limits. These linear models serve as the baseline for a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network, which is tasked with learning only the residual many-body \emph{correlations} on top of the physical model. We develop active important sampling methods driven by these models, which direct the Monte Carlo chains toward undersampled permutation regions, to efficiently reduce the variance in the observable.   We apply this framework to small experiments on benchmark systems: the spin-polarised uniform electron gas, and electrons in a 2D harmonic confining potential. In both cases we demonstrate that this inference-based framework can extract stable energies in regimes where direct Monte Carlo sampling fails due to the sign problem.
summary: This paper tackles the notorious Fermion sign problem in PIMC by reframing the calculation as a statistical inference task. It develops sophisticated machine learning models, such as LSTMs, trained on permutation families to learn the underlying sign structure. This approach allows for stable and accurate energy extraction even in strongly correlated regimes where traditional Monte Carlo methods fail.
main_problem: The primary challenge is overcoming the Fermion sign problem encountered when calculating fermionic observables using path-integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) simulations.
main_result: The proposed statistical inference framework successfully extracts stable energy estimates in regimes where direct ratio estimation fails due to severe sign fluctuations, demonstrating robustness across benchmark systems.
method: The authors recast the calculation as a statistical inference problem, training machine learning models (like LSTM networks) on permutation families derived from Monte Carlo samples, guided by physical priors.
model_or_system: The work applies to fermionic systems simulated via PIMC, focusing on modeling the sign structure associated with exchange permutations within conjugacy classes ('permutation-families').
key_observables: Fermionic energy ($\langle \hat{E} angle_F$), average sign ($\langle \sigma angle_B$), and cycle-count vectors $\mathbf{C}$ characterizing permutation families.
important_parameters: System parameters include particle number ($N$), density regimes (low/high), temperature proxies, and simulation steps (e.g., $10^6$ to $300 	imes 10^6$).
main_assumptions: The methodology relies on imposing physical understanding as inductive priors within a Bayesian framework, treating the problem as an inference task rather than a direct ratio calculation.
figures_summary: Tables present numerical results for energy and sign estimates across varying simulation steps and system parameters ($N=7$ vs $N=33$), comparing different model fits (Linear, LSTM) against raw estimators.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the failure of direct ratio estimation to developing a statistical inference framework based on permutation families. It details specific modeling techniques (MaxEnt, MAP, LSTM) and validates them through applications to electron gas models.
why_interesting: This work provides advanced computational tools for simulating interacting quantum many-body systems where sign problems are prohibitive, offering insights into the limitations of current numerical methods in condensed matter theory.
